stem: Write the Lewis dot structure of CO molecule.
solution:
**Step 1.** Count the total number of valence electrons of carbon and oxygen atoms. The outer (valence) shell configurations of carbon and oxygen atoms are \(2s^2\,2p^2\) and \(2s^2\,2p^4\) respectively. The valence electrons available are \(4 + 6 = 10\).

**Step 2.** The skeletal structure of CO is written as: C O

**Step 3.** Draw a single bond (one shared electron pair) between C and O and complete the octet on O; the remaining two electrons are the lone pair on C. This gives \(:\text{C}\!-\!\ddot{\text{O}}:\) with lone pairs on both atoms.

This does not complete the octet on carbon, and hence we have to resort to multiple bonding — in this case a triple bond — between C and O atoms. This satisfies the octet rule condition for both atoms.

The Lewis dot structure of CO is therefore \(:\text{C} \equiv \text{O}:\), a triple bond with one lone pair on carbon and one lone pair on oxygen.

stem: Write the Lewis structure of the nitrite ion, \(\text{NO}_2^-\).
solution:
**Step 1.** Count the total number of valence electrons of the nitrogen atom, the oxygen atoms and the additional one negative charge (equal to one electron). With \(\text{N}(2s^2\,2p^3)\) and \(\text{O}(2s^2\,2p^4)\):

\(5 + (2 \times 6) + 1 = 18\) electrons.

**Step 2.** The skeletal structure of \(\text{NO}_2^-\) is written as: O N O

**Step 3.** Draw a single bond (one shared electron pair) between the nitrogen and each of the oxygen atoms, completing the octets on the oxygen atoms. This, however, does not complete the octet on nitrogen if the remaining two electrons constitute a lone pair on it.

Hence we have to resort to multiple bonding between nitrogen and one of the oxygen atoms — in this case a double bond. This leads to the Lewis dot structure in which one N–O linkage is a double bond and the other a single bond, the negative charge residing on the singly bonded oxygen:

\([\,\ddot{\text{O}} = \ddot{\text{N}} - \ddot{\text{O}}:\,]^-\) or, equivalently, \([\,:\ddot{\text{O}} - \ddot{\text{N}} = \ddot{\text{O}}\,]^-\)

The nitrogen also carries a lone pair, and the two structures are equivalent canonical forms.

stem: Explain the structure of \(\text{CO}_3^{2-}\) ion in terms of resonance.
solution:
The single Lewis structure based on the presence of two single bonds and one double bond between carbon and oxygen atoms is inadequate to represent the molecule accurately, as it represents unequal bonds. According to the experimental findings, all carbon to oxygen bonds in \(\text{CO}_3^{2-}\) are equivalent.

Therefore the carbonate ion is best described as a resonance hybrid of the three canonical forms I, II and III, in which the C=O double bond is placed in turn on each of the three oxygen atoms while the other two oxygen atoms each carry a single bond and a negative charge.

The actual ion is the resonance hybrid of these three canonical forms, and in it all three carbon–oxygen bonds are identical.

The experimentally determined carbon to oxygen bond length in \(\text{CO}_2\) is \(115\,\text{pm}\). The lengths of a normal carbon to oxygen double bond (C=O) and a carbon to oxygen triple bond (C≡O) are \(121\,\text{pm}\) and \(110\,\text{pm}\) respectively.

The carbon–oxygen bond lengths in \(\text{CO}_2\) (\(115\,\text{pm}\)) lie between the values for C=O and C≡O. Obviously, a single Lewis structure cannot depict this position, and it becomes necessary to write more than one Lewis structure and to consider that the structure of \(\text{CO}_2\) is best described as a hybrid of the canonical or resonance forms I, II and III.
